items.t: Adults: major depressive disorder; neuropathic pain; prophylaxis of chronic tension-type headache; prophylaxis of migraine. Children 6 years and over: nocturnal enuresis after organic causes are excluded and all other drug and non-drug treatments have failed.

items.t: Start low and increase gradually. Initially 25 mg twice daily (50 mg daily); if needed increase by 25 mg every other day up to 150 mg daily in two divided doses. Maintenance: lowest effective dose. Effect usually after 2 to 4 weeks; continue usually up to 6 months after recovery.

src.q: Adults Initially 25 mg 2 times daily (50 mg daily). If necessary, the dose can be increased by 25 mg every other day up to 150 mg daily divided into two doses.
The antidepressant effect usually sets in after 2 - 4 weeks.
usually up to 6 months after recovery in order to prevent relapse

items.t: Over 65 years or cardiovascular disease: initially 10 mg to 25 mg daily, increase up to 100 mg to 150 mg daily in two divided doses as tolerated. Doses above 100 mg: use with caution.

src.q: Elderly patients over 65 years of age and patients with cardiovascular diseas e Initially 10 mg - 25 mg daily

items.t: Start 10 mg to 25 mg in the evening; increase by 10 mg to 25 mg every 3 to 7 days as tolerated. Usual dose 25 mg to 75 mg daily in the evening (once daily or two divided doses). A single dose above 75 mg is not recommended; doses above 100 mg with caution. Effect normally after 2 to 4 weeks; reassess regularly.

items.t: Stopping: withdraw gradually over several weeks.

items.t: Nocturnal enuresis: 6 to 10 years 10 mg to 20 mg (suitable dose form needed); 11 years and over 25 mg to 50 mg daily. Increase gradually; give 1 to 1.5 hours before bedtime. src.q: Concomitant treatment with MAOIs (monoamine oxidase inhibitors) is contra-indicated

items.t: Arrhythmias and severe hypotension are likely at high doses and can occur at normal doses in pre-existing heart disease. QT prolongation reported: caution with significant bradycardia, uncompensated heart failure or QT-prolonging drugs; hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia and hypomagnesaemia raise the risk.

src.q: Cardiac arrhythmias and severe hypotension are likely to occur with high dosage. They may also occur in patients with pre-existing heart disease taking normal dosage.
Caution is advised in patients with significant bradycardia, in patients with uncompensated heart failure, or in patients concurrently taking QT-prolonging drugs.
Electrolyte disturbances (hypokalaemia, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia) are known to be conditions increasing the proarrythmic risk.

items.t: Use with caution in: convulsive disorders, urinary retention, prostatic hypertrophy, hyperthyroidism, paranoid symptoms, advanced liver or cardiovascular disease, pyloric stenosis and paralytic ileus. Narrow anterior chamber angle: acute glaucoma may be provoked.

src.q: This medical product should be used with caution in patients with convulsive disorders, urinary retention, prostatic hypertrophy, hyperthyroidism, paranoid symptomatology and advanced hepatic or cardiovascular disease, pylorus stenosis and paralytic ileus.
In patients with the rare condition of shallow anterior chamber and narrow chamber angle, attacks of acute glaucoma due to dilation of the pupil may be provoked.

items.t: Hyperthyroidism or thyroid medication: great care (arrhythmias). Elderly are particularly prone to orthostatic hypotension.

src.q: Great care is necessary if amitriptyline is administered to hyperthyroid patients or to those receiving thyroid medication, since cardiac arrhythmias may develop.
Elderly patients are particularly susceptible to orthostatic hypotension.

items.t: Surgery: anaesthetics may increase arrhythmia and hypotension risk. If possible stop several days before surgery; otherwise tell the anaesthetist.

src.q: If possible, discontinue this medicinal product several days before surgery; if emergency surgery is unavoidable, the anaesthetist should be informed that the patient is being so treated.

items.t: Suicidal thoughts/behaviour: monitor closely, especially early in treatment, after dose changes, under 25 years and with prior suicidality.

src.q: Close supervision of patients and in particular those at high risk should accompany drug therapy especially in early treatment and following dose changes.

items.t: Bipolar illness: a switch to mania may occur; stop amitriptyline if a manic phase starts.

src.q: In manic-depressives, a shift towards the manic phase may occur; should the patient enter a manic phase amitriptyline should be discontinued.

items.t: Serotonin syndrome with other serotonergic drugs (MAOIs, SSRIs, SNRIs, certain opioids such as tramadol or buprenorphine, other TCAs): can be life-threatening. Use with caution with SSRIs; observe carefully if combined.

src.q: Amitriptyline should be used with caution in patients receiving SSRIs
may lead to serotonin syndrome, which can be life-threatening condition

items.t: Diabetes: may change insulin and glucose responses; antidiabetic therapy may need adjustment.

src.q: amitriptyline may modify insulin and glucose responses calling for adjustment of the antidiabetic therapy in diabetic patients

items.t: Severe skin reactions including DRESS (mostly within 2 to 6 weeks): warn the patient; stop at once if signs appear and never restart.

src.q: At the time of prescription patients should be advised of the signs and symptoms and monitored closely for cutaneous reactions.
Amitriptyline should be withdrawn immediately, treatment with Amitriptyline must not be restarted in this patient at any time

items.t: Hyperpyrexia reported with anticholinergic or neuroleptic drugs, especially in hot weather. Abrupt stopping after long use may cause withdrawal symptoms. Lactose: not for hereditary galactose intolerance, lactase deficiency or glucose-galactose malabsorption.

src.q: Hyperpyrexia has been reported with tricyclic antidepressants when administered with anticholinergic or with neuroleptic medications, especially in hot weather.

src.q: With MAO inhibitors (non-selective as well as MAO A-selective (moclobemide) and MAO B-selective (selegiline)) - risk of "serotonin syndrome"

items.t: Not recommended: sympathomimetics such as adrenaline, ephedrine, phenylephrine (including in anaesthetics and nasal decongestants); centrally acting antihypertensives such as clonidine and methyldopa (review all antihypertensive therapy).

src.q: Combinations that are not recommended Sympathomimetic agents : Amitriptyline may potentiate the cardiovascular effects of adrenaline, ephedrine, isoprenaline, noradrenaline, phenylephrine, and phenylpropanolamine
Tricyclic antidepressants may counteract the antihypertensive effects of centrally acting antihypertensives such as guanethidine, betanidine, reserpine, clonidine and methyldopa.

items.t: Anticholinergic drugs: avoid (paralytic ileus, hyperpyrexia).

src.q: concomitant use of these should be avoided due to an increased risk of paralytic ileus, hyperpyrexia, etc.

items.t: QT-prolonging drugs (e.g. quinidine, some antipsychotics, sotalol, halofantrine): more ventricular arrhythmias. Methadone: caution. Diuretics that cause hypokalaemia (e.g. furosemide): caution.

src.q: may increase the likelihood of ventricular arrhythmias when taken with tricyclic antidepressants
Caution is also advised for co-administration of amitriptyline and diuretics inducing hypokalaemia (e.g. furosemide)

items.t: Tramadol: higher risk of seizures and serotonin syndrome, and possible opioid toxicity (raised tramadol levels).

src.q: Concomitant use of tramadol (a CYP2D6 substrate) and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), such as amitriptyline increases the risk for seizures and serotonin syndrome.

items.t: Fluconazole and terbinafine raise tricyclic levels; syncope and torsade de pointes have occurred.

src.q: Antifungals such as fluconazole and terbinafine increase serum concentrations of tricyclics and accompanying toxicity. Syncope and torsade de pointes have occurred.

items.t: Strong CYP2D6 inhibitors (e.g. fluoxetine, paroxetine, bupropion): marked rise in amitriptyline levels; consider TCA levels and dose adjustment. Duloxetine (moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor): caution.

src.q: These drugs may produce substantial decreases in TCA metabolism and marked increases in plasma concentrations.
Caution is advised in the case of co-administration of amitriptyline with duloxetine, a moderate CYP2D6 inhibitor.

items.t: Diltiazem, verapamil, cimetidine, methylphenidate may raise TCA levels; strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ketoconazole, itraconazole, ritonavir) may interact. Fluvoxamine: avoid.

src.q: Cimetidine, methylphenidate and calcium-channel blockers (e.g. diltiazem and verapamil) may increase plasma levels of tricyclic antidepressants and accompanying toxicity.
Clinically relevant interactions may be expected with concomitant use of amitriptyline and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors such as ketoconazole, itraconazole and ritonavir.

items.t: Inducers (oral contraceptives, rifampicin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, St John's wort) may lower amitriptyline levels and response. The St John's wort herbal SPC says do not take it with tricyclics.

rules.action: Do not use together. Start amitriptyline 14 days after an irreversible MAOI (1 day after moclobemide); start an MAOI 14 days after amitriptyline.
